title: Language and Undertow
premise: Ansel Galloway, a piano tuner who reads houses like sheet music, has spent thirty years renting rooms and avoiding attachments. When he finds a mailbag of undelivered letters hidden behind a wardrobe in a condemned house he's been hired to assess, he learns the letters were stolen by the house's late caretaker—his own estranged father—and that one letter concerns a woman who spent years wrongly imprisoned because it never arrived. As demolition looms, Ansel must deliver what his father withheld, confront the town that remembers both Galloways, and decide whether a man built for transience can finally belong somewhere. The story ends with Ansel staying: he buys the house next door to the prison, opens a small letter-reading service for the illiterate and the isolated, and plays the restored piano on the porch each evening.
about_author: Jonah Yarrow is the pen name of a former postal inspector turned novelist who lives in a converted sorting office on the Atlantic coast. Language and Undertow is their second novel, following a widely praised debut about a lighthouse keeper's widow.

chapters.title: The Pitch of Empty Rooms
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. He tunes a piano in the Marrow House, a condemned Victorian slated for demolition, and describes how he hears history in radiators and floorboards. He keeps every relationship temporary by design. Emotional beat: loneliness disguised as professional detachment.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Moving the wardrobe to check the wall, he uncovers a canvas mailbag stuffed with yellowed letters, all postmarked decades ago and never delivered. The top one is addressed to a name he half-recognizes from childhood. Emotional beat: curiosity curdling into dread.

chapters.title: Inventory of the Undelivered
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV, with flashbacks. In his rented room he sorts forty-one letters by date and address, realizing they span nine years and that the handwriting on the bag's repair stitches matches his father's. Emotional beat: the past arriving uninvited.

chapters.title: What the Neighbors Remember
chapters.summary: Ansel visits Odette Brann, an elderly former neighbor, who recalls his father Raymond as the block's beloved handyman—and mentions the scandal that made the Galloways leave overnight. She refuses to say more. Emotional beat: the first crack in Ansel's curated ignorance.

chapters.title: A Name in the Register
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. At the county records office he traces the addressee: Vera Okonkwo, convicted in 1989 of arson at the cannery, released after eleven years when evidence surfaced too late to matter. One undelivered letter was her alibi witness's reply. Emotional beat: guilt by inheritance.

chapters.title: The Tuner's Rule
chapters.summary: Vera's POV. Now running a laundromat two towns over, Vera receives Ansel's cautious phone call and hangs up. We learn she rebuilt her life by refusing to look backward. Emotional beat: guarded fury meeting cowardly hope.

chapters.title: Letters I Shouldn't Read
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Unable to stop himself, he reads the letters chronologically, watching a love affair and a wrongful conviction unfold through other people's words. His father's theft begins to look less like malice than fear. Emotional beat: complicity.

chapters.title: Raymond's Hands
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Raymond's POV, 1991. Raymond, the building's caretaker, intercepts the letters to protect his brother—the actual arsonist—and tells himself he'll deliver them someday. Emotional beat: the birth of a lifelong lie.

chapters.title: Demolition Date
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. The city confirms the Marrow House comes down in six weeks; salvage crews will strip it first. Ansel realizes the letters are legally found property and the house itself is his only witness. Emotional beat: a deadline becomes a moral clock.

chapters.title: Laundromat, 6 A.M.
chapters.summary: Alternating Ansel and Vera POV. Ansel shows up in person; Vera lets him fold towels while he talks. She doesn't forgive him, but she takes the letter naming her alibi witness. Emotional beat: the smallest possible opening.

chapters.title: The Witness Who Waited
chapters.summary: Vera's POV. Vera tracks down Dolores Finch, the witness whose reply letter never came, and learns Dolores wrote three times before giving up and moving away, ashamed. Emotional beat: grief for a life rerouted by silence.

chapters.title: Brother's Keeper
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. He finds his uncle Cecil living in a trailer park, dying and unrepentant. Cecil admits the arson casually, assuming Ansel came for money. Ansel leaves without a confession on tape but with the truth confirmed. Emotional beat: disgust and a terrible clarity.

chapters.title: Found Family, Borrowed Kitchen
chapters.summary: Ensemble chapter, rotating POV among Ansel, Vera, and Odette. Vera starts feeding Ansel dinner as he helps her draft a petition for exoneration; Odette joins as witness-hunter. A makeshift household forms around a kitchen table. Emotional beat: belonging sneaking up on all of them.

chapters.title: The State's Long Memory
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. A skeptical innocence-project lawyer takes the case but warns that a dead thief, a dead witness's relocation, and a demolished crime scene make proof nearly impossible. Emotional beat: hope with a cost attached.

chapters.title: What Houses Keep
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Salvage crews begin gutting the Marrow House; Ansel rescues the piano and, behind a radiator, finds Raymond's unsent confession letter, written and never mailed. Emotional beat: the father finally speaking from beyond the wardrobe.

chapters.title: Reading Aloud
chapters.summary: Vera's POV. Vera reads Raymond's confession aloud to the group; Odette corroborates details from memory. They realize the letter alone won't suffice—they need Cecil's signature or a deathbed statement. Emotional beat: resolve hardening into strategy.

chapters.title: Trailer Park Vigil
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ansel sits with the dying Cecil for three days, tuning nothing, saying little, until Cecil signs a notarized admission in exchange only for Ansel's promise to bury him under his mother's name. Emotional beat: mercy extended to someone undeserving.

chapters.title: Undertow
chapters.summary: Climax, part one. At the exoneration hearing, the state challenges the confession's validity; Vera testifies about the eleven lost years, and Ansel publicly names his father's theft, surrendering any claim to family reputation. Emotional beat: justice demanded outside the law's convenience.

chapters.title: The Gavel and the Wrecking Ball
chapters.summary: Climax, part two. The court vacates Vera's conviction the same week the Marrow House falls. Ansel watches the demolition holding the last undelivered letter—his father's apology to him, addressed to a son who no longer needs it. Emotional beat: release and mourning braided together.

chapters.title: Deliveries
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. He hand-delivers the remaining letters to descendants across the county, each doorstep a small reckoning. Some recipients slam doors; one elderly woman kisses his hands. Emotional beat: restitution as practice, not event.

chapters.title: A Tenant No Longer
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ansel buys the small house beside the old prison site, moves his tools and the rescued piano in, and hangs a shingle: reading and writing help, no questions asked. Vera paints the porch; Odette claims the rocking chair. Emotional beat: chosen permanence.

chapters.title: Tuning the Future
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Ansel's POV, one year later. Evening lesson night: neighbors' children learn piano while adults learn to read their own mail. Ansel tunes the instrument and listens to the new house speak—radiators, joists, laughter. Emotional beat: quiet joy, identity rewritten in his own hand.
